primary.w: Auto/Auto negotiation; Zephyr says covered by auto-test

step4.objective:
• A port with no pluggable present defaults to automatic speed and duplex negotiation.
  • Inserting a supported pluggable results in successful autonegotiation and link establishment.
  • A port configured for Auto speed and duplex establishes a link with a compliant link partner.
  • Link establishment succeeds when one side is set to Auto and the partner is forced to a supported speed or duplex.
  • An incompatible or unsupported partner configuration causes negotiation to fail predictably — no link is established (or it is correctly reported as down) — rather than settling into an inconsistent or unstable state.
  • The port accurately reports Auto mode together with the negotiated speed and duplex values.
  • Link status is correctly reported as up once autonegotiation completes.
  • After a change that affects negotiation, the port renegotiates and re-resolves cleanly to a valid outcome, without retaining stale negotiated state.
  • Automatic speed and duplex negotiation produces a working link across all supported configurations with a compliant partner.

provenance.objective_response:
• With both link partners set to auto-negotiation, the link comes up at the highest speed and duplex mutually supported by the two ports.
  • An auto-configured copper port resolves cable polarity automatically (auto-MDI/MDIX), establishing the link regardless of straight-through or crossover cabling.
  • Auto/auto negotiation succeeds across copper 10-Gig SFP, fixed copper 1-Gig, and 1-Gig fibre media, each settling at its highest mutually supported rate.
  • A port advertising auto against a partner pinned to a fixed speed converges on that fixed speed where the negotiated result is a supported combination.
  • A port advertising auto against a partner pinned to a fixed duplex converges on a duplex compatible with that partner.
  • Half-duplex is never the negotiated outcome at gigabit or higher rates; only full-duplex results are advertised and resolved at those speeds.
  • Unsupported or mismatched fixed/fixed combinations produce a predictable failure — no link or a link at a safe fallback rate — rather than an inconsistent or oscillating state.
  • Operational speed, duplex and negotiation state reported by the port reflect the actually resolved link and agree between the two partners.
  • Auto-negotiation support, enabled status, advertised capability and resulting operational MAU type are observable both locally and, via the remote partner, through the LLDP IEEE 802.3 MAC/PHY TLVs.
  • Renegotiation after a media, speed or duplex change re-resolves cleanly to the new highest mutually supported combination without a stale reported state.

steps.description: Note: Related ART Tests linked in Traceability.
With no pluggable present, confirm the port defaults to automatic speed and duplex negotiation. Insert a supported pluggable and confirm autonegotiation completes and the link establishes.
Set the port to Auto for speed and duplex with a compliant partner also on Auto. Confirm the link establishes and the port reports Auto mode together with the negotiated speed and duplex.

Vary the partner across supported configurations — both sides Auto, and one side Auto with the partner forced to a supported speed or duplex. Confirm the link establishes and negotiation resolves correctly in each case.

Configure the partner with an incompatible or unsupported speed/duplex setting. Confirm negotiation fails predictably — the link does not come up (or is correctly reported as down) — and the port does not enter an unstable or inconsistent state.

On an established auto-negotiated link, introduce a change that affects negotiation — for example reconfiguring the partner, or removing and re-inserting a supported pluggable — and confirm the port renegotiates and re-resolves cleanly, with reported speed, duplex and link status reflecting the new outcome and no stale state retained.

Auto/Auto link negotiation is the kind of behaviour that automated checks can reasonably confirm at the level of a link reaching an established state with the expected negotiated speed and duplex. Even assuming such coverage exists, the less well-covered areas are typically the negotiation transients and edge conditions — renegotiation after link flaps, mismatched or forced peer settings, and behaviour across cable or media changes — along with the observability that a manual tester relies on, such as advertised-capability exchange, negotiation status reporting, and log or counter evidence that the outcome was genuinely auto-negotiated rather than defaulted. Until a concrete automated test is identified, this should be treated as an unverified coverage gap rather than confirmed automation. ## Rules - The FIRST step is injected server-side as a traceability note — DO NOT generate it. - Generate ONLY the subsequent verification steps exercising the objective's artefacts. - Cover each major objective bullet: positive, negative, special conditions, reporting. - Keep each step high-level enough to be reusable across platforms, but specific enough to be testable. Naming exact values, counts and timings is the PyTest script's job, not this one — a manual step that dictates them narrows the tester to one way of exercising the feature instead of leaving them to produce evidence that it works. - LEAVE `expectedResult` EMPTY on every step. This is deliberate, not an omission. The tester reads the objective and the step and reasons out what should happen; stating the outcome narrows them to producing exactly that result instead of evidence that the feature works. The objective already carries the expected outcomes. - Say WHAT is being exercised, not which command to type. Proving the step was taken — capturing `show` output as evidence — is the generated PyTest script's job, and naming commands or device registers here invents mechanisms that may not exist and narrows the tester besides. - Where a step depends on topology, say which roles it needs (e.g. two links between the DUT and a partner), never a device model or a port number. - Platform-agnostic language: no product names, no hardcoded port strings. ## Output format — this example IS the specification; match its level of detail [ { "description": "Verify LLDP operation with the DUT and its link partner both running default timers. Confirm neighbours are discovered on the test link and that each side reports the other's chassis and port identity.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Vary the transmit interval and hold multiplier across their supported range, including the minimum and maximum. Confirm advertisements are sent at the configured rate and that the neighbour's advertised lifetime tracks the configured values.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Set the transmit interval below the supported minimum and above the supported maximum. Confirm the DUT rejects both and retains its previous configuration.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Disable LLDP transmit on the DUT while leaving receive enabled, then re-enable it. Confirm the neighbour ages out and is rediscovered, and that the port reports the change.", "expectedResult": "" } ] Output the JSON array ONLY. No prose, no markdown fence.
